quote: 14.2.2 At-Will Termination by PB. PB may terminate this Agreement at any time after SFJ has paid or incurred a total of $60 million of Development Costs and prior to the date of receipt of the first Regulatory Approval upon [***] prior written notice to SFJ.
rationale: Both limbs of the rule fail the fallback. (1) Our convenience exit: Section 14.2.2 is the only at-will right we have and it is double-gated — unavailable until SFJ has paid or incurred $60 million of Development Costs and unavailable at all once the first Regulatory Approval is received — and its price is "three hundred percent (300%) of Development Costs paid or incurred by SFJ prior to such termination". In a multi-year term that is effectively no usable convenience right, and the exit charge is far beyond the fallback's cap of roughly three months' fees. (2) SFJ's exit: Sections 14.2.6 (Change of Control of PB) and 14.2.10 (JSC decision disagreement) each let SFJ "in its sole discretion, terminate this Agreement in its entirety at any time" with no stated notice period, and 14.2.3 permits immediate termination on a Material Adverse Event — a counterparty walk-away on fewer than 90 days' notice, which the playbook treats as walk-away territory. We proposed the fallback rather than the preferred position because the existing bargain is a development-financing structure in which SFJ funds the trials against Approval Payments, so a no-penalty 30-day exit would be disproportionate: instead we make PB's at-will right exercisable at any time on 90 days' notice, cut the exit payment to the 150% multiple SFJ itself already accepts in Sections 14.2.6 and 14.2.8.1, and impose a 90-day notice floor on SFJ's discretionary terminations. verification.notes: Primary limb is a genuine fallback failure: PB's only at-will exit (14.2.2) is double-gated (unavailable until SFJ has spent $60M and lost once first Regulatory Approval is received) and priced at 300% of Development Costs, so in a multi-year development term there is effectively no usable customer convenience right and the exit charge far exceeds the fallback's fee cap — correctly classified as a deviation, not an acceptable fallback. Redline is directionally correct and reasonably scoped: it removes the spend/approval gates, sets a 90-day notice (within the fallback band), and reduces the exit payment to the 150% multiple the counterparty itself already accepts in 14.2.6/14.2.8.1 — an internally sourced benchmark that is defensible where a literal '3 months' fees' cap has no analogue in a development-financing structure. Counterparty-exit edits are minimal and on-point: adding a 90-day prior written notice floor to SFJ's 'sole discretion, at any time' terminations in 14.2.6 and 14.2.10 addresses the walk-away trigger (vendor convenience exit on fewer than 90 days' notice) without deleting the negotiated triggers. Failed deterministic checks are not substantive: the 'Customer convenience termination present' regex misses because the customer is named 'PB' rather than 'Customer', and the 0.656 changed-character ratio on p0755 reflects the rewrite the rule genuinely requires (removing gates and repricing the exit fee), with the remainder of the clause left intact. Comment is accurate and appropriately framed (cites the $60M gate, 300% multiple, and SFJ's no-notice discretionary rights; explains the 150%/90-day fallback), and the rationale correctly avoids double-flagging Section 6.7 buy-out pricing under a payments rule. Minor, non-fatal points to flag to the drafter rather than grounds for failure: SFJ's 14.2.6/14.2.10 rights are event-triggered rather than pure convenience rights, so the 'walk-away' characterization is somewhat stretched; and deleting the pre-Approval limit in 14.2.2 leaves the 'obtains Regulatory Approval following such termination' proviso not obviously covering a post-approval exit, which the counterparty may argue lets PB escape Approval Payments.

quote: 9.1 Accounting. Each Party will maintain materially complete and accurate accounting records related to this Agreement in accordance with GAAP. Each Party will retain such records for [***] after the earlier of expiration or early termination of this Agreement.
rationale: SFJ has no audit, inspection or verification right against PB, so there is nothing for this rule to constrain. Article 9 (Records) imposes only mutual record-keeping/retention obligations on "Each Party" and grants neither Party a right to inspect or audit the other's books. The only "Audits" provision, Section 3.6, is each Party auditing the facilities of its own Permitted Third Parties (3.6.1) and PB auditing its own manufacturing facilities (3.6.2), with report copies shared — that is self-audit and reporting, not an SFJ audit of PB. Section 3.5.5 is reciprocal source-data verification of clinical records each Party is itself responsible for. Article 3.18.2 requires PB to deliver financial statements and hold periodic executive review meetings, but confers no examination right, no on-site inspection and no access to PB systems; Articles 4, 6 and 7 contain no cost- or payment-verification audit. There is no unannounced or unlimited audit right and no remote/system access language anywhere in the document, so nothing approaches walk-away territory. Because the absence of any audit right binding us is more favourable than the preferred position, we do not propose inserting frequency, notice or cost-allocation limits (or an audit right) — doing so would create a right against our client that SFJ does not currently have. Noted for the file only: if SFJ later seeks a records-audit right (e.g., over Development Costs or Approval Payments), we should condition it on once per 12 months, 30 days' written notice, business hours, an independent auditor bound by confidentiality, SFJ's cost unless underpayment exceeds 5%, and no access to PB systems.

verification.notes: Claimed status is 'compliant' and the rendered redline is identical to the original paragraphs with no comment — consistent with a compliant, evidence-only finding where no negotiation issue is raised. The cited text supports the conclusion: Art. 9 imposes only mutual record-keeping/retention duties on 'Each Party' with no examination or inspection right; Sections 3.6.1–3.6.2 are each Party's quality oversight of its own Permitted Third Parties / PB's own manufacturing facilities with report copies shared, i.e. self-audit and reporting rather than an SFJ audit right over PB. No unlimited/unannounced audit or remote system-access language appears in the cited clauses, so nothing reaches walk-away territory; the absence of any audit right binding our client is more favourable than the preferred position and correctly left unredlined (inserting limits would create a right SFJ does not have). The failed 'audit frequency limited' deterministic check is a false signal here — the regex cannot match frequency caps because there is no audit right against us to cap; it does not undermine the substance. Rationale appropriately notes for the file the terms to demand (once per 12 months, 30 days' notice, independent auditor, Vendor cost unless >5% underpayment, no system access) if SFJ later seeks a records-audit right.

quote: 15.9 Governing Law. The construction and validity of this Agreement and the provisions hereof, and the rights and obligations of the Parties hereunder, will be governed by the internal laws of the State of Delaware, USA, and, to the extent applicable to Patents and Trademarks, the applicable federal laws of the USA, in each instance without regard to conflict of laws principles.
rationale: Section 15.9 selects Delaware law, which sits squarely at the playbook fallback (Delaware or California law) rather than the preferred New York law. The dispute forum is also within accepted territory: after Executive Officer escalation, disputes go to ICDR arbitration with the seat/legal place of arbitration in New York, governed by the U.S. Federal Arbitration Act (15.10.2.2), so there is no foreign law, foreign venue, or arbitration seated abroad — the walk-away triggers are absent. IP ownership/validity/enforceability disputes are expressly reserved to a U.S. federal court and either Party may seek preliminary injunctive relief in any court of competent jurisdiction (15.10.1). The only shortfalls against the preferred position are Delaware rather than New York law and a domestic arbitral forum rather than New York County courts; both are non-material sub-elements noted here rather than redlined, and the arbitration provisions are symmetrical and do not disadvantage us.

quote: enter into a new subordination agreement with a new lender(s) on terms and conditions that are taken as a whole not less favorable in any material respect to SFJ than those set forth in the subordination agreement to be entered into with SVB
rationale: Searches for MFN/best-terms language (most favoured, no less/not less favourable, at least as favorable, best price, match, comparable terms) returned no pricing or best-terms MFN in the Agreement. The only "not less favorable to SFJ" language is Section 7.5 (p0543), which is a condition on any replacement lender subordination agreement in the security-interest package, not an obligation for PB to extend SFJ the benefit of better terms granted to third parties. Article 6 (Payments to SFJ) and the Licensing Transaction definitions/Section 7.5.5 (p0552) impose consent and approval mechanics on PB's third-party licensing, but no obligation to offer SFJ terms no less favourable than those given to others or to match third-party offers. This meets the preferred position (no MFN obligation on PB), so no redline is proposed.

quote: PB shall notify SFJ in writing of the total amount of Development Costs (inclusive of all Development Costs paid or incurred since the Effective Date) that PB elects to have SFJ fund (the "Elected Total Amount"), which shall be no less than $110 million and no more than $120 million.
rationale: This is a development-funding agreement, not a supply arrangement, and it contains no minimum purchase commitment, take-or-pay obligation, shortfall penalty or volume cap on PB. The spending commitments run the other way: SFJ commits to fund up to $120M of Development Costs (Sections 4.1–4.2), which under the detection guidance is a commitment made to us and is not flagged. PB's payments to SFJ (Article 6 Approval Payments) are purely contingent on obtaining Regulatory Approval and are expressly proportional to actual amounts funded — Section 6.2 scales the Approval Payments by actual Development Costs over $120M and provides for "true-up payments," i.e. a true-up rather than a penalty, which meets the preferred/fallback economics. PB also retains exits: the buy-out options in Sections 6.7.1–6.7.2 and at-will termination under Section 14.2.2. Noted but not flagged as deviations: (i) the $110M floor on the Elected Total Amount in Section 4.2.3(ii) is a minimum draw of funding PB receives (with corresponding consideration trued up under Section 6.2), not committed spend with a shortfall charge; (ii) the matched-spend covenant in Section 4.2.3 ("PB shall spend at least an amount equal to the amount of funding paid by SFJ") is a use-of-proceeds covenant on money PB has received; and (iii) the 300% exit payment on at-will termination is a termination-economics point addressed under the termination rule and is not double-flagged here.

quote: 15.16 Nonsolicitation. During the Term and for a period of [***] thereafter, neither Party shall solicit an employee of the other Party who is or has been involved in the performance or oversight of any of the development activities hereunder to terminate his or her employment and accept employment or work as a consultant with the soliciting Party. Notwithstanding the foregoing, nothing herein shall restrict or preclude the Parties' right to make generalized searches for employees by way of a general solicitation for employment placed in a trade journal, newspaper or website.
rationale: Section 15.16 is the only personnel restriction binding PB; searches for "hire", "employ or engage" and "induce" return no no-hire or broader covenant elsewhere. The clause sits at our fallback position on every material term: it is fully mutual ("neither Party"), scope is narrowed to employees "who is or has been involved in the performance or oversight of any of the development activities hereunder" rather than all personnel, it prohibits only solicitation (no no-hire — PB remains free to hire an SFJ employee who approaches it), and it carries an express general-advertising carve-out for "generalized searches ... by way of a general solicitation for employment placed in a trade journal, newspaper or website". Two minor sub-elements fall short of the preferred position and are noted rather than flagged: the tail duration is redacted ([***]) so it cannot be confirmed against the 24-month walk-away threshold, and it runs from expiry of the Term rather than from the end of the individual's involvement; there is also no separate express carve-out for unsolicited approaches, though the "solicit ... to terminate" framing already leaves employee-initiated contact unrestricted. Since our preferred position (no non-solicit on Customer) is not met but the fallback is satisfied on all material terms, this is compliant and we should not redline it. If the redacted tail proves to exceed 24 months, that would be a separate walk-away issue to raise on the unredacted copy.

quote: 13.6.2 EXCEPT AS OTHERWISE SET FORTH IN THIS ARTICLE 13, NEITHER PARTY MAKES, AND EACH PARTY EXPRESSLY DISCLAIMS, ANY REPRESENTATION OR WARRANTY OF ANY KIND WITH RESPECT TO THE SUBJECT MATTER OF THIS AGREEMENT, EITHER ORAL OR WRITTEN, EXPRESS, IMPLIED, STATUTORY OR OTHERWISE, INCLUDING ANY REPRESENTATION OR WARRANTY REGARDING THE USE, RESULTS OR EFFICACY OF THE PRODUCT.
rationale: This is a co-development/funding agreement, not a software or services procurement: PB (our party) is the performing/development party and SFJ is principally the funder, with SFJ acting as sponsor and performing trial activities in the SFJ Territory. Article 13 contains express, largely mutual warranties that cover the elements the playbook cares about on the counterparty side — authority and no conflicting agreements (13.1.1–13.1.2), compliance with law (13.1.3 Anti-Corruption Laws; 13.1.4 debarment certifications; 13.1.5 required certifications, permits and authorisations), and SFJ's funding-capacity warranty (13.5). SFJ's performance standard is set by Section 2.2.2, which requires it to conduct the Clinical Trials and perform all other assigned responsibilities in compliance with the Protocol, all Applicable Laws and the Agreement, and "Applicable Laws" expressly includes GCP/GLP/GMP and ICH guidelines — the industry-standard equivalent of the "professional and workmanlike" standard in this context. Critically, the disclaimer does not swallow the express warranties: 13.6.2 opens "EXCEPT AS OTHERWISE SET FORTH IN THIS ARTICLE 13", so this is not walk-away "AS IS" territory. The 13.6.1 no-warranty on trial outcome/patentability is mutual and, because PB generates the Research Results, operates in our favour, so we do not disturb it. The conformance-period and repair/replace/refund mechanics (12 months / 90 days) have no analogue here as there are no software deliverables; that gap is noted rather than flagged, and remedies for breach run through Article 12 indemnification and Article 14 termination. PB's own warranties are more extensive than SFJ's, but that is the negotiated funding bargain and is addressed under the reps/diligence rules rather than this warranty rule. No redline proposed.

The rationale correctly declines to disturb 13.6.1 (mutual, and favourable to our party as generator of Research Results) and PB's broader warranties, in line with the rule against flagging clauses that benefit our party or duplicating terms covered by other rules.
